1.title: Governance Roles, Training and Approaches
1.text: Welcome to Module two: Governance Roles, Training and Approaches. This module covers competency B of domain one. It answers four practical questions. Who does what in an A I governance program? Who needs to be trained, and on what? How should the approach fit the organization? And how do developers, providers, deployers and users differ?

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do five things. Define the roles and responsibilities of A I governance stakeholders. Build cross-functional collaboration into the program. Create a training and awareness program for every stakeholder group. Differentiate governance approaches by size, maturity, sector and risk tolerance. And tell developers, providers, deployers and users apart by their governance duties.

1.title: Case Check-In: Who Owns What at Helios?
1.text: At Helios, Samira Haddad, the Chief A I Officer, must stand up an A I governance committee. Meanwhile, Lucia Moreno's recruiters will use the hiring tool every day, and nobody has trained them on it. Veridex supplies the tool, and Helios uses it in its own hiring. Your job is to say who decides, who advises, who checks, and who gets trained.

1.title: Who Does What in AI Governance
1.text: Start with the roles. The board and executives set strategy and risk tolerance, provide resources, and take responsibility for decisions about A I risk. That is N I S T subcategory Govern two point three. The A I governance committee and the Chief A I Officer set policy, approve high-risk use cases and track the inventory. Legal and privacy interpret laws and run impact assessments. Security and risk test threats and run the risk process. H R, business owners and data science train people, own use cases, and build the systems. Exam tip: read a role question as a duty question.

1.title: The Three Lines Applied to AI
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. The I I A's Three Lines Model is a common way to organize roles. The governing body is accountable to stakeholders and ensures effective structures. The first line delivers the product or service and manages risk: business owners, product teams and data science. The second line provides expertise, support, monitoring and challenge: risk, compliance, legal, privacy, security and the A I governance office. The third line is internal audit, giving independent assurance. Exam tip: independent assurance means internal audit, not the committee that wrote the policy.

1.title: What Legal, Privacy, Security, Risk and HR Each Bring
1.text: Each function brings a distinct duty. Legal tracks A I and sector law and reviews contracts and claims, as Jonas Weber does with the Veridex agreement. Privacy handles lawful basis, notices, data subject rights and impact assessments. Security protects models, data and pipelines and tests for attacks. Risk and compliance run the risk process and monitor policy. H R handles training, role changes and fair use in hiring. And the business owner owns the use case, its outcomes and its risk. Exam tip: the business owner owns the risk. The others advise and check.

1.title: Accountability in Writing
1.text: Accountability has to be written down. N I S T asks that roles, responsibilities and lines of communication for A I risk be documented and clear to everyone. That is Govern two point one. Executive leadership takes responsibility for decisions about A I risk, Govern two point three. Document decision rights: who proposes, who approves, and who can stop a system. Name an escalation path from the team to the committee to the board. Define roles for human oversight, Govern three point two. A responsibility matrix keeps roles from blurring. Exam tip: unclear responsibility is fixed with documented roles and escalation.

1.title: Cross-Functional Collaboration
1.text: A I risk cuts across law, data, security, people and product, so no single function can govern it. A cross-functional committee brings those views to each decision. N I S T says decision-making should be informed by a diverse team, Govern three point one. To make collaboration work, give the committee a charter, a regular cadence, a clear intake route for new use cases, and an escalation path. And give it decision rights, not only advice. Exam tip: collaboration is judged by effect. Every use case is reviewed from every angle before approval.

1.title: A Range of Expertise and Viewpoints
1.text: N I S T asks for teams diverse in demographics, disciplines, experience, expertise and backgrounds. Different disciplines catch different risks: lawyers see liability, engineers see failure modes, and H R sees fairness. Affected people, such as candidates, customers and frontline staff, see harms that builders miss. Silos hide risk: a model approved by data science alone may never meet legal or privacy review. At Helios, the committee adds recruiters and support leads, and it listens to candidate and customer feedback. Exam tip: to improve effectiveness, widen who is in the room.

1.title: Training and Awareness: Who Needs What
1.text: The training program covers A I terminology, strategy and governance, and each audience needs a different mix. Executives need strategy, risk tolerance and accountability. Builders need governance requirements, documentation, testing and bias. Business users and recruiters need to know how the tool works, its limits, and when to escalate. Legal and procurement need laws, vendor terms and third-party risk. All staff need the basics, acceptable use, and how to raise a concern. Exam tip: one generic course for everyone is the wrong answer.

1.title: The AI Literacy Duty in the EU AI Act
1.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide, tagged dates and verify live. Article four of the E U A I Act applies to providers and deployers of A I systems, whatever the risk level. It has applied since the second of February, twenty twenty-five. As now worded, they take measures to support A I literacy of staff and others operating A I for them, considering knowledge, experience, education, training, the context of use and the people affected. It does not require guaranteeing a specific level for any individual. The Digital Omnibus rewrote the Article; before, it asked them to ensure, to their best extent, a sufficient level. As of the twenty-seventh of October, twenty twenty-six, check the consolidated text.

1.title: Building a Training Program That Works
1.text: A training program that works is a cycle. First, assess needs: who uses, builds, buys and oversees A I, and what each group knows. Second, design by role, with short, practical modules in the language of the audience. Third, deliver and record, keeping attendance as evidence. Fourth, check understanding with quizzes and scenarios, not only completion. Fifth, refresh when systems, rules or incidents change what people must know. N I S T Govern two point two asks that personnel and partners be trained for their duties. Exam tip: training is a cycle, not an event.

2.title: Fitting the Approach to the Organization
2.text: Governance has to fit the organization. Size: a small firm uses a named owner and light process, while a large one uses a committee and several lines. Maturity: early programs start with an inventory and basic policy, while mature ones add metrics, audits and automation. Industry: regulated sectors add sector rules on top of A I rules. Products and services: systems that affect rights or safety need stronger controls. Objectives and risk tolerance set thresholds and the amount of review, Govern one point three. Exam tip: a comparison question wants a fit, never no governance at all.

2.title: Governance Operating Models
2.text: Three operating models are worth knowing. Centralized: one team sets and runs governance for all A I. It suits smaller or highly regulated organizations, but can become a bottleneck. Federated, or hub and spoke: a central team sets policy and business units run their own A I within it. It suits large, diverse organizations, but practice can be uneven. Decentralized: each unit governs itself. That suits only the earliest stage, and it leaves gaps. Helios uses a hybrid. Exam tip: for a large company with many units, hybrid is the usual answer.

2.title: The Actors in the AI Chain
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. The Body of Knowledge asks you to tell four actors apart. The developer designs, builds and trains the model or system. The provider places the system on the market or puts it into service under its own name, often the developer, sometimes not. The deployer uses the system under its own authority in its operations. The user interacts with the system or its output, and may be an employee or a member of the public. Importers and distributors sit in the supply chain. Exam tip: one company can hold several roles, so assign the role per system.

2.title: The AI Act's Names for the Roles
2.text: This is a beyond-the-Body-of-Knowledge slide. Article three of the E U A I Act defines the roles. A provider develops a system or general-purpose model, or has one developed, and places it on the market under its own name or trademark. A deployer uses a system under its authority, except for personal non-professional use. An authorized representative holds a written mandate from a provider. An importer places on the Union market a system bearing a third-country name. A distributor makes a system available without being provider or importer. Operator is the umbrella term. Exam tip: the Act says deployer, not user.

2.title: Responsibilities, Opportunities and Needs by Role
2.text: Each role has its own responsibility, opportunity and need. Developers document design and test for bias and safety; they can build governance in from the start, and they need clear requirements and quality data. Providers meet legal duties and supply instructions; they can earn trust with transparent products, and need feedback on use and incidents. Deployers fit the system to the use and oversee it; they can choose vendors on evidence, and need documentation from the provider. Users use the system as intended and report problems; they need training and a way to complain. Exam tip: ask providers for information in the contract.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Let us recap. Roles: leadership decides risk tolerance, the committee sets policy, functions advise, business owners own use cases, and audit assures. Collaboration is diverse and cross-functional, with a charter, a cadence and decision rights. Training is by audience, covers terminology, strategy and governance, and is a cycle, with the Article four duty in the E U. The approach fits size, maturity, sector, products, objectives and risk tolerance. And the actors are developer, provider, deployer and user, assigned per system.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. Samira Haddad wants independent assurance, reporting to the board, that Helios's A I governance and risk management are adequate and effective. Which function should provide it? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Independent assurance is the third line, internal audit. The builders and the committee that wrote the policy cannot independently assure their own work.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. Which responsibility belongs to executive leadership in an A I governance program? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Executive leadership sets risk tolerance and takes responsibility for decisions about A I risk. Labeling data, running dashboards and drafting documentation are operational tasks for the teams.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. A company's A I governance committee has only data scientists and one lawyer, and use cases are approved with little challenge. Which two additions would best improve its effectiveness and range of expertise? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are B and D. A privacy specialist and a business owner bring new disciplines and the user's view. More of the same adds little, and a voting vendor is a conflict.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A company plans A I training for recruiters, developers, executives and buyers, and must also meet the E U A I literacy duty. Which plan best meets the stakeholders' needs? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. Role-based training covers terminology, strategy and governance, matched to each group's knowledge and context. The E U duty reaches providers and deployers whatever the risk level, so a one-off video or developer-only course falls short.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A forty-person startup uses a third-party chatbot, and a multinational bank deploys credit-scoring models. How should their governance approaches differ? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. The startup uses light, risk-based controls under a named owner, and the bank uses a formal committee, several lines and a stricter risk tolerance. A uniform approach over-burdens one and under-protects the other.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. Helios uses the Veridex hiring tool under its own authority to screen applicants. Veridex makes the tool available under its own name. Which two statements describe the roles correctly? Select two. The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and C. The party that makes the system available under its own name is the provider, and the organization that uses it under its own authority is the deployer.

2.title: Answers at a Glance
2.text: Here are all six answers. Question one: C. Question two: B. Question three: B and D. Question four: D. Question five: A. Question six: A and C. That completes Module two. Next, Module three turns to policies and procedures across the whole A I life cycle, including third-party risk.
